mfa_reminder.title: Enable 2FA everywhere!
mfa_reminder.desc: Use an authenticator app or hardware key when available. Avoid SMS if you have a stronger option.

passwords.title: Accounts & Authentication
passwords.subtitle: Secure your digital identity with Managers, MFA, and Passkeys.

quick.title: If you only do one thing today
actions: Install a password manager and import your top 5 accounts.
Enable MFA on email + bank (avoid SMS; use an app).
Download and store backup codes offline (print or password manager secure note).

why_manager.title: Why use a Password Manager?
why_manager.desc: Humans are bad at creating random passwords. Computers are great at it. A password manager generates and stores unique, complex passwords for every account.

bitwarden.desc: Best default for most users: open-source clients, strong free tier, and broad device support.

proton.desc: Alternative if you're already in the Proton ecosystem.

apple.desc: Apple ecosystem option. Works across Apple devices and via Chrome extension on other platforms.

desktop.title: Desktop (Windows / Mac)
steps: 1. Go to bitwarden.com and create a free account.
2. Install the Bitwarden browser extension for Chrome, Edge, or Firefox.
3. Log in to the extension.
4. Turn off your browser's built-in password saving to avoid confusion.

mobile.title: Mobile (iOS / Android)
steps: 1. Download the Bitwarden app from the App Store or Play Store.
2. Log in with your account.
3. CRITICAL: Go to Phone Settings -> Passwords (or Auto-fill Service) -> Select Bitwarden.
4. Now Bitwarden can automatically type passwords into your apps.

recovery.title: Recovery & backup codes
items: Download and store MFA backup codes offline (print or password manager secure note).
Keep a second authenticator app/device enrolled when possible.
Set a unique recovery email that also has MFA.
recovery.note: Lose the backup codes? You may need to contact support with identity verification—some services won't let you disable MFA without codes. This is why storing them safely matters.

bad_passwords.title: Stop Using These Passwords
bad_passwords.desc: If you use any of these, change them immediately:

good_passwords.title: What "good" looks like
good_passwords.desc: Long, unique, and generated by your manager. For passphrases, combine 4–5 random words.

questions.prompt: What’s the biggest risk of using SMS for MFA?
options: SIM swap attacks can steal your number
questions.correct: SIM swaps are common; use app or hardware MFA instead.
questions.explainer: SMS relies on carriers; attackers can hijack your number.

questions.prompt: Best place to store backup codes?
options: Password manager secure note or printed offline
questions.correct: Store them offline or in a secure note, not in plain email/photos.
questions.explainer: Email/photos are easy targets if the account is compromised.

questions.prompt: How many accounts should share the same password?
questions.correct: Reuse = chain breach. Use unique, manager-generated passwords.
questions.explainer: One breach shouldn’t open every other account.

mfa.title: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
mfa.subtitle: The single most important setting to enable.
mfa.intro: MFA adds a second lock to your account. Even if a hacker steals your password, they can't get in without the second key.

sms.title: SMS (Text Messages)
sms.desc: AVOID. Vulnerable to SIM swapping attacks where hackers steal your phone number.

apps.title: Authenticator Apps
apps.desc: Good default. Scan a QR code, get a new 6-digit code every 30 seconds, and keep access even when offline.

hardware.title: Hardware Keys (YubiKey)
hardware.desc: Maximum Security. A physical USB key you plug in. Phishing-proof but costs $50+. Important: Register at least 2 keys as backup in case you lose one.

biometrics.title: Biometrics
biometrics.desc: Fingerprint or FaceID. Convenient, often used as a second factor on mobile devices.

app_recommendation.desc: 2FAS is free, open-source, works on iOS and Android. No account needed. Syncs between devices via iCloud/Google backup. Simple, no bloat.

bitwarden_advanced.title: Advanced Bitwarden Features
bitwarden_advanced.otp: Bitwarden Premium can generate MFA codes (TOTP). This is convenient but creates a single point of failure—if your vault is compromised, attackers get both your password and MFA. For highest security, use a separate authenticator app.
bitwarden_advanced.passkeys: Bitwarden can now store Passkeys, allowing you to sync them across all your devices, not just Apple or Google ones.

quick_actions.title: Fast wins
items: Email, bank, and cloud storage should always have MFA with an app or hardware key.
Avoid SMS unless no other option. If forced to use SMS, set a PIN with your carrier to reduce SIM-swap risk.
Store backup codes offline and label them by service.

gmail.title: Gmail MFA Setup
steps: Go to 'Manage your Google Account' -> 'Security'.
Click '2-Step Verification' -> 'Get Started'.
Choose 'Authenticator App' (Recommended). Avoid SMS.
Scan the QR code with 2FAS or another trusted authenticator app.
Enter the 6-digit code to verify.
CRITICAL: Download Backup Codes and store them offline.

proton.title: Proton Mail MFA Setup
steps: Go to Settings -> 'Account and password'.
Click 'Enable two-factor authentication'.
Scan QR code with your authenticator app.
Enter the 6-digit code.
SAVE the recovery codes shown. This is mandatory.

passkeys.title: Passkeys: The Future
passkeys.desc: Passkeys replace passwords with cryptographic keys stored on your device. You login with biometrics (fingerprint, face) or your device PIN.
passkeys.setup: To setup on Google: Go to g.co/passkeys and click 'Use passkeys'.
notes: Passkeys work best when you’re signed into the same account on phone + laptop (Apple ID, Google, or Microsoft).
On shared computers, stick to passwords + MFA instead of passkeys.
Passkey portability is improving but not universal. Some platforms now support export (e.g., to Bitwarden), but check before relying on it.

browsing.title: Safe Browsing
browsing.subtitle: Take back your privacy. Block trackers and ads.

extensions.title: Essential Extensions
extensions.intro: Install these on every browser you use.

ublock.title: uBlock Origin
ublock.desc: The best ad and tracker blocker. Uses very little memory.

privacy_badger.title: Privacy Badger
privacy_badger.desc: Learns to block invisible trackers automatically. By EFF.

quick_settings.title: Copy/paste settings to harden any browser
items: Disable third-party cookies.
Turn on HTTPS-Only mode.
Block pop-ups and auto-play media.
Turn off telemetry/usage reporting.

browsers.title: Secure Browsers
browsers.brave: Good default for daily browsing. Blocks ads and trackers out of the box.
browsers.firefox: Good alternative. Requires manual hardening for best privacy.
browsers.tor: For maximum anonymity only. Slow. Don't use for regular browsing.

questions.prompt: Why enable HTTPS-Only mode?
options: It forces encrypted connections to prevent snooping
questions.correct: HTTPS encrypts your connection, protecting against interception on public networks.
questions.explainer: Without HTTPS, anyone on the same network could potentially see your traffic.

questions.prompt: What's the safest way to install browser extensions?
options: From official browser stores and trusted publishers only
Download .zip files and drag them in
questions.correct: Official stores have some vetting; random sources can ship malware.
questions.explainer: Even official stores aren't perfect, so stick to well-known, trusted publishers.

questions.prompt: When should you use Tor Browser?
options: For sensitive browsing where anonymity matters
questions.correct: Tor is for anonymity, not speed or convenience. Avoid logging into personal accounts.
questions.explainer: Tor routes traffic through multiple relays, which is slow but hides your identity.

brave.title: Brave setup (2 min)
steps: Settings -> Privacy & security: enable aggressive tracker/ad blocking.
Settings -> Privacy: enable "Clear browsing data on exit" for cookies.
Disable Google services (autofill, web services you don’t need).

firefox.title: Firefox setup (3 min)
steps: Settings -> Privacy: choose "Strict".
Enable HTTPS-Only mode in all windows.
about:config -> set telemetry to false (toolkit.telemetry.enabled).

tor.title: Tor basics (2 min)
steps: Use for sensitive browsing only; avoid logging into personal accounts.
Keep Security Level at "Safer" or "Safest" for less fingerprinting.
Do not resize the window or install extensions.

social.title: Social Media & Messaging
social.subtitle: Secure your communications and protect your data on public networks.

e2e_explanation.title: What is End-to-End Encryption (E2EE)?
e2e_explanation.desc: Imagine sending a letter in a locked steel box. You have the key, and only the recipient has the key. The mailman (the app server) delivers the box but cannot open it. That is E2EE. Standard messaging is like a postcard—anyone handling it can read it.

signal.title: Signal - The Gold Standard
signal.desc: Best default for private conversations: end-to-end encrypted, open source, nonprofit, and designed to keep server-side metadata minimal.

whatsapp.desc: Messages are end-to-end encrypted by default, but WhatsApp is owned by Meta and collects more metadata than Signal.

metadata.title: Metadata that apps keep
points: Signal: minimal metadata stored (message content and contacts protected; only registration date and last connection may be disclosed if legally compelled).
WhatsApp/iMessage: metadata like who/when can be collected.
SMS: no encryption; assume everything is visible to carrier.

verification.title: Verify safety numbers/keys (Signal)
steps: Open chat -> tap name -> "View safety number".
Scan or compare digits with the person in real time.
Tap "Verified" so you get alerts if it changes (possible hijack).

vpn.title: VPN Services
vpn.intro: A VPN encrypts traffic between your device and the VPN server, which is especially helpful on public WiFi. It hides your IP from websites, while your ISP can still see that you're using a VPN. Choose reputable, audited providers.
vpn.mullvad: Strong privacy-focused choice. No email needed; the account is a number. Flat €5/month as of June 2026.
vpn.proton: Good free tier if you're in the Proton ecosystem. Swiss-based, no-logs.
vpn.ivpn: Privacy-focused alternative. No email required. Transparent company.

explanation.title: How does a VPN work?
explanation.desc: A VPN (Virtual Private Network) creates a secure 'tunnel' between your device and a VPN server. It masks your IP from sites you visit and makes local-network snooping much harder, while your ISP typically sees the VPN connection itself.

wifi.title: Do this on public Wi‑Fi
wifi.donts_title: Avoid doing this on public Wi‑Fi
items: Use a VPN to reduce what the network operator can see and mask your IP address from sites.
Turn on HTTPS-Only in your browser.
Forget the network when done; turn off auto-join.
donts: Don't assume public Wi-Fi is private. HTTPS helps, and a VPN reduces what the network operator can see.
Avoid logging into sensitive accounts without HTTPS or a VPN.
Don't share files over AirDrop/Bluetooth unless needed.

email.title: Private Email
email.why: Gmail integrates with Google's ecosystem and your emails are not end-to-end encrypted. With Proton Mail, emails between Proton users are end-to-end encrypted.

proton.desc: Strong privacy-focused email. Stored mail uses zero-access encryption, and mail between Proton users is end-to-end encrypted.

gmail.desc: Gmail is convenient and secure, but standard email is not end-to-end encrypted by default. Use a privacy-focused account for sensitive mail.

questions.prompt: Why is Signal recommended over WhatsApp?
options: Signal doesn't share metadata with Meta and is truly private
questions.correct: Signal is non-profit, doesn't collect metadata, and doesn't share data with advertising companies.
questions.explainer: WhatsApp is owned by Meta and shares metadata for profiling, even though messages are encrypted.

questions.prompt: When should you use a VPN?
options: On public WiFi and to hide browsing from your ISP
questions.correct: VPNs protect you on public WiFi and reduce what your ISP can inspect directly by encrypting traffic to the VPN server.
questions.explainer: Without a VPN, your ISP can usually see the services/domains you connect to and any unencrypted traffic. Public WiFi is especially risky.

questions.prompt: What does end-to-end encryption (E2EE) protect against?
options: The app's server reading your messages
questions.correct: E2EE means only you and the recipient can read messages—not even the app company.
questions.explainer: With E2EE, the server just passes along encrypted data it cannot decrypt.

devices.title: Device Security
devices.subtitle: Secure your mobile devices and desktop computers.
checklist_items: Enable screen lock (6-digit PIN or biometric)
Disable lock screen notifications for sensitive apps

resilience.title: Resilience checklist
items: Full-disk encryption on (FileVault, BitLocker, Android/iOS default).
Automatic cloud backups enabled (iCloud/Google Drive/OneDrive).
Set updates to automatic for OS and browser.

lost_device.title: If your device is lost/stolen
steps: Use Find My / Find My Device to lock and locate, then erase if unrecoverable.
Change passwords for email + banking first; revoke old sessions.
Notify your carrier (SIM swap risk) and your bank if applicable.

questions.prompt: Why enable full-disk encryption?
options: Protects data if the device is lost/stolen
questions.correct: Encryption keeps data unreadable without your key/PIN.
questions.explainer: Physical loss is common; encryption limits damage.

questions.prompt: What to do first if a phone is stolen?
options: Use Find My to lock/erase and change passwords for email/bank
questions.correct: Lock/erase remotely and secure key accounts immediately.
questions.explainer: Fast action reduces account takeovers.

questions.prompt: Where should backups live?
questions.correct: Off-device backups protect against loss, theft, or ransomware.
questions.explainer: Local-only backups are lost with the device.

phishing.subtitle: Don't take the bait. Learn to spot fake emails and scams.

urgency.title: Urgency
urgency.desc: Claims you must act immediately (e.g., 'Account suspended').

greeting.title: Generic Greeting
greeting.desc: Uses 'Dear Customer' instead of your name.

attachment.title: Unexpected Attachment
attachment.desc: Invoices or receipts you didn't ask for.

checklist.title: Email Security Checklist
items: Enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) on your email account.
Use a unique, strong password (generated by a password manager).
Never click links in suspicious emails. Go to the site directly.
Check the sender's actual email address, not just the display name.

tips.title: Micro-tips to stay safe
items: Hover or long-press links to reveal the real URL before clicking.
When in doubt, open a new tab and type the site yourself.
Unexpected invoices/attachments? Call the sender on a known number first.

sample.title: Example phishing email (what to notice)
sample.subject: Subject: URGENT - Account Suspended
sample.body: Hi, your account will be closed in 12 hours. Download the attached invoice or log in here.

after_click.title: If you already clicked
steps: If you entered credentials: Change the password immediately and enable MFA. This is the most urgent step.
Revoke sessions/devices on that account; check recent activity for unauthorized access.
If you entered credit card info, call the bank to block/replace the card.
If you downloaded a file: Disconnect from Wi-Fi and run an antivirus scan.

questions.prompt: An email says your account will be closed in 1 hour and the button opens paypa1-support.com. What is the best action?
options: Hover, spot the fake domain, delete, then go directly to paypal.com
questions.correct: Right—never click, use a trusted URL you type yourself.
questions.explainer: Avoid engaging. Go direct to the real site or app.

questions.prompt: A coworker sends an unexpected invoice attachment. What’s safest?
options: Call/message them on a known channel to confirm before opening
questions.correct: Verification on a separate channel stops most phish attempts.
questions.explainer: Never open surprise attachments before confirming.

questions.prompt: You clicked a phishing link and entered credentials. What first?
options: Change that account’s password and enable MFA immediately
questions.correct: Resetting access + MFA is the most urgent step.
questions.explainer: Contain the account right away; then review activity.

other_channels.title: Beyond Email: Other Phishing Channels
other_channels.intro: Attackers don't just use email. Watch out for these too:

smishing.title: SMS Phishing (Smishing)
smishing.desc: Fake texts claiming to be from banks, delivery services, or government. Never click links in unexpected texts—go directly to the official website or app.

vishing.title: Phone Call Phishing (Vishing)
vishing.desc: Callers pretending to be tech support, banks, or officials. They create urgency ('Your account is compromised!'). Hang up and call the official number yourself.

quishing.title: QR Code Phishing (Quishing)
quishing.desc: Malicious QR codes placed over legitimate ones (parking meters, restaurant menus). Before scanning, check if the code looks tampered with. Preview the URL before opening.

encryption.title: How encryption protects you
encryption.intro: Think of encryption as a lock on your data. Without the key, it's unreadable gibberish.

items.name: One key (symmetric)
items.desc: Like a safe with one key. You lock your data, and only someone with the same key can open it. Your phone uses this to protect everything when locked.

items.name: Two keys (asymmetric)
items.desc: Like a mailbox: anyone can drop a letter in (public key), but only you have the key to open it (private key). This is how secure websites work.

items.name: Hashing (fingerprints)
items.desc: Creates a unique 'fingerprint' of data. Used to check if files are tampered with, and to store passwords safely—websites store the fingerprint, not your actual password.

items.name: E2E vs regular encryption
items.desc: Regular: like a sealed bag—the mail carrier can't read it in transit, but the post office (server) can open it. E2E: like a locked box inside the bag—only you and the recipient have keys.

takeaways: The tools we recommend (Signal, Bitwarden, Proton) handle encryption for you—just use them.
Never share recovery phrases or backup codes. Treat them like cash.
If your device is lost/stolen and was unlocked, or you suspect someone knows your PIN, change your passwords immediately. If it was locked with a strong PIN, encryption protects your data.
Look for 'https://' in the URL—this means the connection is encrypted. But note: this only protects the connection, not the site's legitimacy. Phishing sites can have HTTPS too.

questions.prompt: What does symmetric encryption use?
options: One shared key for both encrypt and decrypt
questions.correct: Symmetric encryption uses the same key to lock and unlock data—like a safe with one key.
questions.explainer: Your phone uses symmetric encryption to protect data when locked.

questions.prompt: Why use a password manager instead of remembering passwords?
options: Password managers are faster to type
Humans can't create truly random, unique passwords for every account
questions.correct: Password managers generate and store unique, complex passwords for each account—something humans can't do reliably.
questions.explainer: Reusing passwords means one breach compromises all your accounts.

questions.prompt: What does HTTPS protect?
options: The connection between you and the website
questions.correct: HTTPS encrypts the connection, but doesn't guarantee the site is legitimate—phishing sites can have HTTPS too.
questions.explainer: Always check the actual domain name, not just the padlock icon.

advanced.title: Advanced Networking
advanced.subtitle: Understand how the internet really works under the hood.

dns.title: How DNS Works
dns.intro: When you type 'google.com', your computer needs to find the actual server address. DNS (Domain Name System) is like the internet's phone book - it translates human-readable names into IP addresses.

osi.title: The OSI Model
osi.intro: The OSI model breaks down network communication into 7 layers. Each layer has a specific job, making troubleshooting and understanding easier. Remember: 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away'.

ports.title: Understanding Ports
ports.intro: Think of your computer as an apartment building. The IP address is the building address, and each port is a different apartment number where different services live.

protocols.title: Network Protocols
protocols.intro: Protocols are the rules computers use to talk to each other. Different protocols serve different purposes - some prioritize speed, others reliability or security.

firewall.title: How Firewalls Work
firewall.intro: A firewall is like a security guard for your network. It checks all incoming and outgoing traffic and decides what to allow or block based on security rules.

tls.title: SSL/TLS Handshake
tls.intro: Before your browser can securely communicate with a website, they perform a 'handshake' to establish trust and agree on encryption. This happens when a secure session is established (for example, first connection or session renewal).

ipv.title: IPv4 vs IPv6
ipv.intro: The internet is running out of IPv4 addresses. IPv6 is the new standard with virtually unlimited addresses, but the transition is still ongoing.

questions.prompt: What does DNS do?
options: Translates domain names to IP addresses
questions.correct: DNS is like the internet's phone book - it converts names you remember to addresses computers understand.
questions.explainer: Without DNS, you'd need to memorize IP addresses like 142.250.185.78 for every website.

questions.prompt: Which OSI layer handles IP addresses and routing?
questions.correct: The Network layer (Layer 3) is responsible for IP addressing and routing packets between networks.
questions.explainer: Routers operate at Layer 3, making decisions based on IP addresses.

questions.prompt: In the apartment building analogy, what is the port number?
questions.correct: The port is like the apartment number - it directs traffic to the right service on a computer.
questions.explainer: IP address = building address, Port = apartment number, Service = resident.

questions.prompt: Why should you always prefer HTTPS over HTTP?
questions.correct: HTTPS uses encryption to protect your data from being read by others on the network.
questions.explainer: Without HTTPS, passwords and personal data travel in plain text anyone can intercept.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a firewall?
options: Filter network traffic based on security rules
questions.correct: Firewalls act as security guards, checking and filtering all network traffic.
questions.explainer: They block unauthorized access while allowing legitimate traffic through.

questions.prompt: What happens during an SSL/TLS handshake?
options: Browser and server establish secure encrypted connection
questions.correct: The handshake establishes trust and encryption before any sensitive data is exchanged.
questions.explainer: A handshake occurs when a secure HTTPS session is established or renewed.

questions.prompt: Why was IPv6 created?
questions.correct: IPv4 only supports about 4.3 billion addresses - not enough for all devices today.
questions.explainer: IPv6 provides 340 undecillion addresses - virtually unlimited.

vpn.title: How a VPN Protects You

steps.title: Without a VPN
steps.text: Everything you do online travels through your internet provider first. It can see the name of every site you visit — your bank, your email, your social apps.

steps.title: Turning the VPN on
steps.text: A VPN wraps your traffic in an encrypted tunnel before it leaves your device — like putting your mail inside a locked box.

steps.title: What your provider sees now
steps.text: Just one thing: an encrypted connection to a VPN server. The list of sites you visit is hidden.

steps.title: The honest catch
steps.text: The sites don’t disappear — now the VPN company can see them instead of your provider. A VPN moves your trust; pick a provider you actually trust.

vpn.why_matters: On public Wi‑Fi (cafés, airports) a VPN also shields you from strangers on the same network.

mfa.title: Authentication factors
mfa.explanation: Authentication factors are different ways to prove your identity. Using 2+ factors means even if one is stolen, attackers still can't get in.
mfa.weak: password alone is easy to steal

steps.title: One lock: just a password
steps.text: A password is something you know — and anything you know can be stolen, guessed, or leaked.

steps.title: Add a second lock: your phone
steps.text: Now a thief with your password still can’t get in — they’d also need the phone in your pocket.

steps.title: Three locks: add your fingerprint
steps.text: Something you know, something you have, something you are. Each extra factor multiplies the attacker’s work.

steps.title: The everyday sweet spot
steps.text: Two factors is the practical minimum for email and banking. Use an authenticator app instead of SMS when you can.

mfa.why_matters: Most account takeovers start with a stolen password. MFA is the single highest-impact switch you can flip.

e2e.title: End-to-End Encryption

steps.title: You write a message
steps.text: “Hello!” is about to leave your phone.

steps.title: Locked before it leaves
steps.text: Your device scrambles the message. Only your friend’s device holds the key to unscramble it.

steps.title: Crossing the internet
steps.text: Everyone in between — Wi‑Fi, provider, even the chat company’s own server — sees only meaningless symbols.

steps.title: Unlocked on arrival
steps.text: Your friend’s device uses its key to turn the symbols back into “Hello!”.

steps.title: Delivered privately
steps.text: Nobody in the middle could read it. That is end-to-end encryption: locked at your end, unlocked at theirs.

steps_regular.title: You write a message
steps_regular.text: “Hello!” is about to leave your phone.

steps_regular.title: Sent readable
steps_regular.text: Without end-to-end encryption, the message travels in a form the chat service can read.

steps_regular.title: The server reads it
steps_regular.text: The company’s server sees “Hello!” in full — and so could an employee, a hacker who breaks in, or anyone they share data with.

steps_regular.title: Delivered
steps_regular.text: Your friend gets the message — but it was readable along the way.

steps_regular.title: The difference
steps_regular.text: Switch to the end-to-end view: the same trip, but nobody in the middle can read a word.

e2e.why_matters: Signal and WhatsApp encrypt end-to-end by default. Regular SMS, email, and many chat apps do not.

tracker.title: Tracker blocking
tracker.explanation_exposed: Without blockers, trackers follow you across websites and build a profile of your interests, habits, and identity.
tracker.explanation_blocked: With a blocker like uBlock Origin, trackers are stopped. No profile is built.
tracker.third_party_desc: Third-party trackers are small pieces of code from outside companies hidden inside websites. When the same company’s tracker sits on many sites, it can follow you across all of them.
tracker.blocker_desc: With a tracker blocker like uBlock Origin, these scripts are blocked. The website still works, but trackers can't collect data.
tracker.blocked_message: No data collected. Your browsing stays private.

steps.title: You read the news
steps.text: A hidden tracker from an ad company loads with the page and quietly notes what you read and for how long.

steps.title: You go shopping
steps.text: The same company’s tracker sits on this site too — it recognizes you and links this visit to your reading habits.

steps.title: You scroll social media
steps.text: Third site, same watchers. Your interests, budget, and friends now sit in one growing profile you never agreed to.

steps.title: Turn on a blocker
steps.text: A tracker blocker (built into Brave, or the uBlock Origin extension) simply refuses to load the hidden watchers.

steps.title: Sites still work
steps.text: Pages load normally — often faster. Only the watching parts are gone.

steps.title: Nothing to sell
steps.text: Each visit stays separate. No profile, no targeted price hikes, nothing for data brokers to trade.

tracker.why_matters: This profile is used to target ads, adjust prices, and is often resold. Blocking trackers is the easiest privacy win there is.

phishing.subject: Subject
phishing.body_text: Your account will be closed in 12 hours unless you verify your identity immediately.
phishing.link_text: Click here to verify your account

steps.title: Check the sender
steps.text: It says PayPal, but the address is paypa1‑billing.com — spelled with the digit 1. Scammers fake addresses that look right at a glance.

steps.title: Manufactured panic
steps.text: “URGENT! 12 hours!” — scams rush you so you act before you think. Real companies almost never threaten deadlines by email.

steps.title: Generic greeting
steps.text: “Dear Customer” — a company you have an account with knows your name. Mass-sent scams don’t.

steps.title: The link lies
steps.text: The button says one thing, but the real destination is a scam site. Hover on desktop or long-press on mobile to preview where a link truly goes.

steps.title: Dangerous attachment
steps.text: invoice_2024.pdf.exe is a program dressed up as a document. One click can hand over your device.

find.hint: Tap every part of this email that looks suspicious.
find.found_all: All 5 found! You’re ready for the real thing.

phishing.why_matters: Phishing is how most people actually get hacked — not by genius hackers, but by one convincing email on a busy day.

dns.title: DNS Resolution
dns.technical_text: DNS uses UDP port 53 for queries. Each step involves a query/response pair. The TTL (Time To Live) determines how long the result is cached. Modern DNS can use encryption (DoH/DoT) to prevent snooping.

1.title: Your device asks its helper
1.detail: You typed google.com, but computers find each other by number (an IP address). Your device asks its helper — the resolver — “what number is google.com?”
1.role: The resolver is like a helpful librarian: it doesn’t know every answer, but it knows exactly where to look.

2.title: Start at the top
2.detail: The librarian first asks a root server — the internet’s front desk. It doesn’t know google.com, but it knows who manages all names ending in .com.
2.role: Root servers are the front desk: they point you to the right department.

3.title: Ask the .com directory
3.detail: The .com directory doesn’t know the number either, but it knows which server holds Google’s own records.
3.role: The TLD server is the catalog for one ending, like .com or .ua.

4.title: The source of truth
4.detail: Google’s own name server gives the definitive answer: 142.250.185.78. It’s authoritative — Google controls it.
4.role: The authoritative server is the author of the record — the one place the answer truly lives.

5.title: Connected — and remembered
5.short: The answer comes back to you
5.detail: The number travels back and your browser connects. The librarian remembers the answer for a while, so next time is instant.
5.role: The whole trip took milliseconds — and you never even saw it.

dns.why_matters: DNS is why changing one setting — your DNS provider — can block ads network-wide or protect a whole family’s devices.

osi.title: OSI Model

steps_down.title: You press Send
steps_down.text: A message starts in an app — your browser, email, or chat. This is the only layer you ever see.

steps_down.title: Translate and seal
steps_down.text: The message is converted to a standard format and encrypted — sealed so outsiders can’t read it.

steps_down.title: Open a conversation
steps_down.text: Both computers agree a conversation is happening and keep track of it.

steps_down.title: Cut into numbered pieces
steps_down.text: Long messages are split into numbered chunks, so lost pieces can be re-sent and order restored.

steps_down.title: Address the envelope
steps_down.text: Every piece gets the destination’s internet address (IP) written on it.

steps_down.title: Hand to the local courier
steps_down.text: Each piece is packaged for the next hop on your local network — your Wi‑Fi router.

steps_down.title: Onto the wire
steps_down.text: Everything becomes radio waves, electrical pulses, or light. Physics takes it from here.

steps_up.title: Signals arrive
steps_up.text: Radio waves or pulses reach the destination and become data again.

steps_up.title: Local delivery checked
steps_up.text: The network card confirms: yes, this is addressed to me.

steps_up.title: Address verified
steps_up.text: The IP address matches — these pieces are for this computer.

steps_up.title: Pieces reassembled
steps_up.text: Numbered chunks are put back in order; missing ones are requested again.

steps_up.title: Conversation resumed
steps_up.text: The pieces are matched to the right ongoing conversation.

steps_up.title: Unsealed and translated
steps_up.text: Encryption is removed and the data returns to a readable format.

steps_up.title: Message appears
steps_up.text: The app shows “Hello!” — the whole round trip took milliseconds.

osi.why_matters: You never see these layers, but they explain tech-support logic: “Is Wi‑Fi on?” is layer 1, “does the site load?” is layer 7. Finding the broken layer is how network problems get fixed.

ports.title: Ports: The Apartment Building

steps.title: Door 80: the old web
steps.text: A visitor knocks on door 80 — plain web pages (HTTP). It works, but conversations through this door aren’t private.

steps.title: Door 443: the secure web
steps.text: Door 443 is the encrypted web (HTTPS) — the padlock in your browser. Most of the internet lives here now.

steps.title: Door 22: the manager’s entrance
steps.text: Door 22 (SSH) lets administrators control the computer from afar. Powerful — and a favorite target for break-ins.

steps.title: Door 25: the mail slot
steps.text: Door 25 (SMTP) is where mail servers hand off email to each other.

steps.title: Door 53: the information desk
steps.text: Door 53 (DNS) answers “what number is google.com?” — the internet’s address-book service.

ports.why_matters: One building (your computer, one IP address) hosts many services — the port number is just which door to knock on. A firewall protects you by keeping unused doors shut.

protocols.title: Protocol Comparison

steps_web.title: Sending a postcard
steps_web.text: Over plain HTTP, your message travels like a postcard — words out in the open.

steps_web.title: Anyone can read it
steps_web.text: On public Wi‑Fi, “anyone” includes the café network and strangers sitting on it.

steps_web.title: Same message, sealed
steps_web.text: HTTPS puts the identical message in a sealed envelope only the website can open.

steps_web.title: The padlock
steps_web.text: That seal is the padlock in your address bar. No padlock — type nothing sensitive.

steps_transport.title: Certified mail
steps_transport.text: TCP numbers every piece and gets a receipt for each. Lost one? It’s re-sent.

steps_transport.title: Everything, in order
steps_transport.text: Web pages, email, and downloads use TCP — being complete matters more than being fast.

steps_transport.title: A quick shout
steps_transport.text: UDP just sends — no receipts, no re-sending. Piece 2 got lost? Keep going.

steps_transport.title: Better dropped than frozen
steps_transport.text: Video calls and games use UDP: losing a frame beats freezing the call.

protocols.why_matters: You don’t choose these — apps do. But the padlock (HTTPS) is yours to check before typing a password.

firewall.title: Firewall Protection

steps.title: The doorman
steps.text: A firewall stands between the internet and your network, checking every connection against its guest list.

steps.title: Secure web? Come in.
steps.text: A visitor for door 443 — the encrypted web — is on the list. Allowed through.

steps.title: Plain web? Fine.
steps.text: Door 80 is allowed too, so ordinary web pages reach you.

steps.title: Telnet? Turned away.
steps.text: Door 23 is an obsolete remote-control entrance with no lock. It’s not on the list — blocked, no exceptions.

steps.title: On duty around the clock
steps.text: Every arriving connection gets the same check, automatically. This is why you leave firewalls on.

firewall.why_matters: Your router and your computer each run a firewall. You rarely notice them — that’s the point.

tls.title: TLS Handshake
tls.why_matters: Without TLS, passwords and personal data travel in plain text anyone can intercept. Always look for the padlock icon in your browser.

1.title: Hello, let’s talk privately
1.detail: Your browser calls the site: “I’d like a private line. Here are the secret-code styles I can speak.”
1.analogy: Like greeting a bank teller and asking for a private room

2.title: Prove who you are
2.detail: The site replies with its certificate — an ID card vouched for by an authority your browser already trusts. Fakes get caught here.
2.analogy: Like checking a passport against the official registry

3.title: Agree on a secret
3.short: A key no eavesdropper can copy
3.detail: Browser and site each mix in a private ingredient and arrive at the same shared secret — without ever sending it. A listener can’t reproduce it.
3.analogy: Like two people mixing paints: everyone sees the colors exchanged, but only they can mix the final shade

4.title: The padlock appears
4.detail: From this moment, everything you send — passwords, cards, messages — is scrambled with that secret. This is what the padlock in your address bar means.
4.analogy: Like switching to a private language only you two speak

tls.technical_text: The steps above are the TLS 1.3 handshake: ClientHello (supported versions and cipher suites), ServerHello with the certificate, a Diffie–Hellman key exchange producing session keys, then symmetric encryption (e.g. AES-256) with integrity checks (HMAC). The whole exchange takes one round trip.

ipv.title: IPv4 vs IPv6

steps.title: Every device needs a number
steps.text: To be reachable, each device gets an internet address — like a phone number: 192.168.1.1.

steps.title: The old system: IPv4
steps.text: IPv4 has about 4.3 billion possible numbers. In the 1980s that felt infinite.

steps.title: We ran out
steps.text: Phones, TVs, watches, doorbells — billions of devices later, IPv4 numbers are exhausted. Devices now often share addresses to cope.

steps.title: The new system: IPv6
steps.text: IPv6 has 340 undecillion addresses — enough to give every grain of sand its own. No sharing required.

ipv.why_matters: Your devices switch between the two automatically — nothing to configure. It’s simply why internet addresses come in two shapes.
